why.B: ~/.claude/commands/ is personal. It works for one developer but never reaches teammates through git, so 'every developer when they clone' fails.
why.C: CLAUDE.md holds always-loaded instructions and context. It can't define a /review command.
why.D: Claude Code has no .claude/config.json with a commands array. It is a plausible-sounding invention.

OFF-04.whenRight: If the checklist were only one developer's personal habit that teammates should not see, ~/.claude/commands/ (B) would be the right home.
OFF-04.trap: 'available to every developer when they clone or pull': the command must live in the repository (.claude/commands/), not in home directories.

why.B: Letting the implementation reveal the boundaries means discovering dependencies after you have already moved code, which is the costly rework plan mode exists to prevent.
why.C: Detailed upfront instructions assume the right service structure is already known. Nobody has explored the dependencies yet.
why.D: Waiting for 'unexpected' complexity ignores that the stem already states it: dozens of files and boundary decisions.

OFF-05.whenRight: For a small, clearly scoped change (a single-file bug fix with a stack trace), direct execution would be the better choice. After the plan is approved, direct execution is also how you implement it.
OFF-05.trap: 'dozens of files' plus 'decisions about service boundaries': stated complexity and architectural choices mean plan mode from the start.

why.B: One root CLAUDE.md with sections loads everything everywhere and relies on Claude inferring which section applies. That isn't deterministic, and it wastes context.
why.C: Skills load on demand, when invoked or when Claude decides they are relevant. The requirement is automatic application based on the file path.
why.D: Directory-level CLAUDE.md files follow the directory tree. Test files spread next to every component can't share one convention source without copies in many folders.

OFF-06.whenRight: If each area's conventions were confined to one directory and no file type spanned directories, subdirectory CLAUDE.md files (D) would work acceptably.
OFF-06.trap: 'spread throughout the codebase' plus 'regardless of location': glob-scoped .claude/rules/ files with paths frontmatter.

why.A: A JSON schema can validate structure, but it doesn't show how a given input should map to the output (which nesting, which timestamp format). Claude still has to guess the transformation.
why.C: More precise prose is still prose. After two inconsistent iterations, a third description is likely to be interpreted differently again.
why.D: Asking Claude to restate its understanding can diagnose the gap, but it doesn't give Claude an unambiguous target for the next attempt.

COM-31.whenRight: If the output shape were already correct and the remaining problem were downstream validation of many responses, a JSON schema check (A) would be a useful guardrail alongside the examples.
COM-31.trap: 'described requirements in prose, but Claude interprets them differently each time': show 2–3 input/output examples instead of more prose.

why.A: Picking webhooks silently makes an architectural choice (one-way, no delivery tracking) that the ambiguous requirement never approved.
why.C: Scaffolding first and deferring the integration decision means writing code whose shape depends on the decision you postponed, which invites rework.
why.D: Choosing bot tokens assumes a need for delivery confirmation that the task doesn't state, and may add infrastructure nobody asked for.

COM-32.whenRight: If the task explicitly said 'use incoming webhooks like the existing one-way channels', direct execution (A) would be appropriate because the approach would already be decided.
COM-32.trap: 'fundamentally different integration approaches' plus 'without specifying': multiple valid approaches with infrastructure implications call for plan mode.

why.A: Moving everything into skills removes the always-on coding standards and testing conventions from automatic loading, so they would depend on invocation.
why.B: @import improves organisation, but imported files load together with CLAUDE.md, so PR, deploy and migration guidance would still load in every session.
why.C: Path-scoped rules attach to file types. PR review, deployment and migration procedures are workflows, not conventions for particular files, so globs don't capture when they are needed.

COM-33.whenRight: If the task-specific guidance were really conventions for particular files (for example, how every migrations/*.sql file must be written), path-scoped rules (C) would be the better fit.
COM-33.trap: 'always follow' versus 'only when doing those tasks': CLAUDE.md for always-loaded standards, skills for on-demand workflows.

why.B: A cheaper or faster model doesn't reduce how much output lands in the main context. The pollution remains.
why.C: Three smaller skills still dump their combined output into the same session, and the analysis becomes fragmented.
why.D: Compressing results inside the same context throws away analysis detail. The 'keeping full analysis capabilities' requirement points to isolation, not truncation.

COM-35.whenRight: If the problem were only cost or latency, not context pollution, a model override (B) would be a reasonable tweak.
COM-35.trap: 'loses the context of the original task' plus 'keeping full analysis capabilities': isolate with context: fork.

why.B: Skill frontmatter has no username-conditional feature, and editing the shared project skill would affect everyone.
why.C: Mechanically it works (a personal skill shadows a same-name project skill), but it silently hides the team version for that developer. The guide's pattern is a different name. This was the community repo's key.
why.D: There is no override frontmatter field. Precedence comes from location, not from a flag.

COM-36.whenRight: If the developer deliberately wanted /commit itself to behave differently for them, and accepted that it silently shadows the team version, a same-name personal skill (C) would work.
COM-36.trap: 'without affecting teammates': the guide's pattern is a personal variant under a different name.
COM-36.note: Answer key changed from the community repo's C to A, to match official guide v1.0 task 3.2 ('personal variants … with different names to avoid affecting teammates').
COM-36.explanation: Guide v1.0 (task 3.2) describes exactly this: a personal variant under ~/.claude/skills/ with a **different name** (e.g. /my-commit), so the team's /commit stays untouched and the personal version is explicit. Personal skills aren't version-controlled, so teammates are unaffected.

why.B: This would explain why the new developer gets *different* behaviour, but the symptom is that the new developer is *missing* guidance the others have, which points to where the guidance lives.
why.C: Claude Code doesn't learn per-user preferences through repetition. Instructions come from memory files that load at session start.
why.D: CLAUDE.md is read fresh in each session. No cache explains a difference between developers on the same up-to-date repo.

COM-37.whenRight: If the new developer had the guidance but behaved differently because of a contradictory instruction in their own ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, cleaning up that user-level file (B) would be the fix. /memory would show it.
COM-37.trap: 'a fourth developer who just joined' plus 'same repo, up-to-date code': the guidance must be in user-level config, so move it to project level.

why.A: Project CLAUDE.md loads in every session, so the endpoint examples would cost context during debugging and review, which is exactly what the stem wants to avoid.
why.B: Pasting examples by hand into every request is unrepeatable and error-prone. A skill packages the same content once for the whole team.
why.C: Path-scoped rules load whenever Claude works with matching files, so debugging or reviewing code in the API directory would still pull in the examples.

COM-38.whenRight: If the content were conventions that apply to every edit of API files (error-handling style, response wrapper), a path-scoped rule (C) would be correct because the need would follow the file, not the task.
COM-38.trap: 'only when creating new endpoints, not when debugging or reviewing ... in the API directory': the trigger is the task, not the path, so use an on-demand skill.

why.A: Positional parameters don't prompt for missing input, @ references don't isolate the skill from earlier conversation context, and a description warning enforces nothing.
why.C: Splitting the skill and adding 'ask if missing' instructions relies on prompt compliance and leaves the context-leak problem (2) unsolved.
why.D: All three fixes are prompt instructions. They are probabilistic and don't isolate context or restrict tools.

COM-39.whenRight: If only problem (1) existed, argument-hint alone would be enough. If only (3) existed, a tool restriction (or, in current docs, disallowed-tools or permission deny rules) alone would be enough.
COM-39.trap: 'fixes all three problems': map each symptom to its configuration key. argument-hint for missing args, context: fork for context leakage, allowed-tools for tool scope.
COM-39.note: Docs nuance: guide v1.0 treats allowed-tools as a restriction. Current Claude Code docs describe allowed-tools as pre-approval (other tools stay callable) and offer disallowed-tools to remove tools. For the exam, B is still correct.

why.A: No .claude/config.yaml mapping mechanism exists. Conditional loading is done with paths frontmatter inside rule files.
why.C: README.md files are not loaded as instructions. Only CLAUDE.md files, .claude/rules/ files and their imports are memory.
why.D: Subdirectory CLAUDE.md files add to their parents rather than overriding them, and they are scoped to directories, not topics. They don't organise topic modules.

COM-42.whenRight: If certain topics applied only to particular file types, adding paths frontmatter to those rule files would turn the topic modules into conditionally loaded rules (task 3.3).
COM-42.trap: 'organize ... into focused topical modules': .claude/rules/ with one Markdown file per topic.

why.A: The ! prefix runs shell commands to inject their output into the skill prompt. It doesn't isolate the brainstorming conversation.
why.C: Start and end marker skills don't remove anything from context. The exploration text stays in the conversation history.
why.D: Moving the skill to personal scope changes who can use it, not where its output goes.

COM-43.whenRight: If the goal were only to stop teammates from seeing an experimental skill, moving it to ~/.claude/skills/ (D) would be the right change.
COM-43.trap: 'subsequent responses are influenced by the alternatives discussion': exploratory output must be isolated with context: fork.

why.A: User scope works per person but gives no shared, version-controlled config. Six developers would maintain six drifting setups.
why.B: A custom wrapper server is over-engineering. .mcp.json already supports ${VAR} expansion, and a community GitHub server already exists.
why.D: Placeholder tokens plus local overrides are fragile. The placeholder can be committed and used by mistake, and overriding project config is extra manual work.

COM-44.whenRight: If only one developer wanted to try an experimental GitHub server, user scope (A, in ~/.claude.json) would be the right place.
COM-44.trap: 'consistent tooling across the team' plus 'without committing credentials': project .mcp.json with ${GITHUB_TOKEN}.
COM-44.note: Docs nuance: current Claude Code docs call the default `claude mcp add` scope 'local' (personal, for this project only, stored in ~/.claude.json) and keep 'user' for personal servers across all projects. Env var expansion also supports ${VAR:-default}.

why.B: /compact summarises after the fact and loses detail. Running discovery in the main context still fills it, and phases 2–3 need clear context for consistent design.
why.C: Headless mode with manual summaries adds orchestration work and breaks the collaborative design phase, which needs an interactive session.
why.D: Batches spread over multiple sessions lose the shared design discussion. CLAUDE.md can carry a pattern but not the nuanced decisions made in phase 2.

COM-45.whenRight: If discovery output were moderate and the session merely getting long, running /compact (B) during extended exploration would be an acceptable lighter step.
COM-45.trap: 'large output ... quickly filling the context window' in phase 1: isolate verbose discovery in an Explore subagent and keep the main context for design and implementation.
